name: Alsace Grand Cru

climate.koppen_name: Temperate, no dry season, warm summer

terms: France's protected place names. A wine sold under one must follow that appellation's rules. The EU's term for the same tier is PDO, or AOP in French.
Indication Géographique Protégée, the tier below AOC. It replaced vin de pays in 2009.
France's simplest category, in use since 2010. It replaced vin de table.
There is no legal or agreed definition of old, so the words promise nothing on their own.
An appellation for 51 named vineyards. The wine must come from one of them, name it on the label, and keep yields to 55 hl/ha or less.
Late harvest. In ripeness rules it sits close to a German Auslese.
Made from grapes with noble rot, close to a German Beerenauslese.

notes: Most Alsace whites come from aromatic grapes, so many are aromatic, floral and spicy.
Riesling here is known for dry wines, and Gewürztraminer for highly aromatic ones.
Alsace was long known for dry wines, but some producers now leave some sugar, and sweetness often follows the house style.
Long, dry autumns let Pinot Gris hang late, often giving very powerful flavors.
Late harvest (VT) Riesling and Muscat tend to be off-dry, while Gewürztraminer and Pinot Gris tend to be sweeter.

blurb.text: Alsace's grand cru tier, first recognized in 1975 and now 51 named vineyards, each its own AOC. Their rules are stricter than Alsace AOC's, including a base yield of 50 hectoliters per hectare for white wine.
